name: Clamp Guard Control
description: Clamp the opponent's shoulder line between your knee and overhook, with wrist control, to create an armbar, triangle, or omoplata dilemma that they cannot escape without giving up a submission entry.
shortInstruction: Knee on shoulder, overhook the arm, control the wrist on the other side — the clamp is a submission waiting to happen.
summary: Clamp guard (also called 'clamp' or 'arm clamp') pins the opponent's arm across your body while your knee blocks their shoulder. This creates a two-on-one on the trapped arm. From here, every reaction they make opens a submission: they posture into the triangle, they pull out into the armbar, they roll into the omoplata.
whyItWorks: By pinning their arm with your knee and overhook, you isolate one arm entirely — they can only defend with the free arm.
The clamp removes their ability to posture, since their head and shoulder are pinned to your chest.
Every escape attempt feeds a different submission — this is the Danaher 'position before submission' principle in action.
The overhook controls their elbow while the knee blocks their shoulder roll — they cannot simply pull free.
commonMistakes: Clamping too low on the arm (at the wrist) instead of at the shoulder — the shoulder pin is what makes the clamp work.
Letting the opponent free their trapped elbow by rotating their arm inward.
Losing the overhook because you relaxed your grip — the overhook must be active and tight.
Not controlling the free hand, allowing them to post and base out of the clamp.
coachingCues: Knee to shoulder, not knee to ribs.
Overhook like you mean it — limp overhooks lose the clamp.
Two arms, one arm — their free arm can't save the trapped one.
Feel the pressure: if they're comfortable, your clamp is wrong.
safetySummary: Do not crank submissions from the clamp — control the position first, then apply the finish smoothly.
Protect your own neck: keep your head tight to their chest, not dangling in a guillotine line.
If they stack you, release the clamp and reset — do not fight the stack with a locked clamp.
keyCorrections: If they pull their arm free, your knee was too low — bring it up to the shoulder line.
If they posture out, you lost the overhook — re-attack the arm before they sit up.
If they roll through the omoplata, control their hip and follow their rotation.

systemLogic.corePrinciple: Secure the clamp (knee on shoulder + overhook + wrist control of free hand) → feel their reaction → attack the open submission.

decisionTree.action: triangle choke. Option 2: They pull the arm out → armbar. Option 3: They roll away → omoplata.
The system is reaction-based: you don't need to force any submission, just maintain the clamp and wait for their movement.

moneyDetails: The knee must be on the shoulder, not floating — if the knee is on their ribs, they can posture and stack you.
Your overhook should capture their triceps against your sternum; a loose overhook at the wrist gives them mobility to escape.
Control their free wrist with your free hand — this prevents them from posting and basing out.
Keep your hips mobile; the clamp is a dynamic position, not a static lock.
nextStep: Master the clamp-to-triangle bridge and the clamp-to-armbar transition to chain your attacks.
fixItFast: Knee keeps slipping? Dig it deeper into the armpit, not the ribs.
Overhook feels weak? Lock your hands around their arm for extra security.
They're stacking you? Release the clamp, frame on their hips, and reset to open guard.
